e-web-66d419e04424.quote: The rapid shift toward agentic and long-context workloads in Large Language Models (LLMs) is pushing the industry beyond the capacity of individual servers toward disaggregated shared storage to handle TB-scale context states. This movement has led to the emergence of specialized shared context layers designed to externalize and share cumulative inference states across distributed clusters. While offloading to a data processing unit (DPU) within just-a-bunch-of-flash (JBOF) architectures accelerates NVMe-over-fabrics (NVMe-oF) target processing, the need for sophisticated software-level optimization and cost-efficiency burdens remain significant. Consequently, the ideal architecture for scaling this shared context infrastructure is still an active area of exploration. In this paper, we propose ITME (Inference Tiered Memory Expansion), which leverages a CXL-hybrid memory to present a massive, TB-scale byte-addressable remote memory expansion. This approach enables cost-efficient scaling and simplifies the software stack through direct byte-addressability, effectively addressing the challenges of shared context infrastructure. Our key insight is that the deterministic access patterns of voluminous model weights and prefix caches enable the system to proactively manage data movement across the memory-storage hierarchy. We validate ITME by evaluating its performance potential with production-grade SK Hynix CMM and PCIe Gen5 NVMe SSDs, while further demonstrating its functional feasibility through an FPGA-based hardware prototype. Overall, ITME enhances conventional CPU-offloading by providing additional remote memory expansion to accommodate large KV cache footprints beyond host memory limits, achieving up to a 35.7% throughput improvement.

e-web-da2a240f4f4b.quote: Addressing the Memory Bottleneck in Large Language Models

e-web-2148e510ec88.quote: The rapid evolution of Large Language Models (LLMs) has shifted the computational challenge from raw processing power to memory capacity. Modern foundation models require hundreds of gigabytes of space simply to store model weights; for example, a model like O P T - 175 B OPT\text{-}175B O P T - 175 B requires approximately 325 GB 325 \text{ GB} 325 GB in FP16 precision. Beyond weights, the emergence of agentic AI and long-context applications has transformed the Key-Value (KV) cache—a dynamic record of previous tokens used to speed up generation—from a temporary buffer into a massive, long-lived state.

e-web-c9715620a1d7.quote: Figure 1: Comparison between a traditional 4-tier memory structure and the proposed ITME architecture which introduces a CXL-Hybrid shared memory tier ( T 3.5 T3.5 T 3.5 ).

e-web-637b8d6f9f48.quote: In standard high-performance inference systems, memory is organized in a hierarchy: high-bandwidth GPU memory ( T 1 T1 T 1 ), host CPU memory ( T 2 T2 T 2 ), local SSDs ( T 3 T3 T 3 ), and remote storage ( T 4 T4 T 4 ). As context lengths grow, T 1 T1 T 1 and T 2 T2 T 2 are frequently exhausted, forcing the system to either recompute lost data or rely on slow storage tiers. Current industry efforts to bridge this gap often use Data Processing Units (DPUs) in specialized storage arrays, but these solutions are costly and involve complex software stacks.

e-web-774027beb945.quote: Inference Tiered Memory Expansion (ITME) offers an alternative by leveraging Compute Express Link (CXL) technology. ITME introduces a CXL-hybrid memory tier ( T 3.5 T3.5 T 3.5 ) that combines the massive capacity of NAND flash (SSDs) with the byte-addressable speed of DRAM. By presenting this hybrid storage as a unified memory space, ITME allows for TB-scale expansion that is both cost-effective and performant.

e-web-616c1f00a4d3.quote: The heart of ITME is the CXL-hybrid memory device. Unlike traditional SSDs that are accessed through block-based file systems, this device is byte-addressable, meaning the CPU or GPU can access it similarly to standard RAM. The hardware architecture integrates high-density NAND flash with a hardware-managed DRAM cache to bridge the significant latency gap between the two.

e-web-5763c3609aa0.quote: Figure 2: The internal hardware architecture of the CXL-Hybrid device, featuring a cache controller, metadata buffer, and SSD/DRAM interfaces.

e-web-b3b414fb7188.quote: To maintain high performance, the device uses an internal DRAM cache (typically 32 GB 32 \text{ GB} 32 GB ) to store the most frequently accessed data from a much larger backend SSD (e.g., 1 TB 1 \text{ TB} 1 TB ). The management of this cache—including checking for hits or misses and handling data movement between the SSD and DRAM—is performed entirely in hardware. This hardware-level management uses an on-chip Metadata Buffer (SRAM) to track cache line states with 16 -way 16\text{-way} 16 -way set associativity.

e-web-87649ca5f0b8.quote: A critical design choice in ITME is the alignment of bandwidth. The hardware is designed to saturate a PCIe Gen5 x8 host interface, which provides roughly 18 GB/s 18 \text{ GB/s} 18 GB/s . By using a 4-channel DRAM and a 2-channel SSD configuration, the path from the SSD to the DRAM cache is also 18 GB/s 18 \text{ GB/s} 18 GB/s . This balance ensures that if the system needs to prefetch data from the SSD into the cache, it can do so at the full speed allowed by the host connection, preventing the storage backend from becoming a permanent bottleneck.

e-web-e6771171ef63.quote: While the hardware provides the capacity, software coordination is required to ensure that the right data is in the DRAM cache exactly when the GPU needs it. ITME achieves this through a custom user-level library and modifications to the vLLM inference framework.

e-web-6e21cd231bc3.quote: ITME provides specific APIs that allow the application to tell the hardware which data to prepare. For instance, the chm_prefetch_object(ptr, size) function allows the system to identify a specific tensor or KV cache block and trigger its migration from the SSD to the DRAM cache. This process is highly efficient, with a software overhead of only 1 - 3 μ s 1\text{-}3 \mu\text{s} 1 - 3 μ s , which is negligible compared to the time required to move large chunks of data.

e-web-e5b263da28df.quote: The ITME implementation within vLLM organizes data movement into a multi-tier pipeline. When the GPU memory ( T 1 T1 T 1 ) is full, KV cache blocks are evicted to a "CPU Staging Buffer" ( T 2 T2 T 2 ). These blocks are gathered into large contiguous chunks (e.g., 512 MB 512 \text{ MB} 512 MB ) before being transferred to the remote CXL-hybrid memory ( T 3.5 T3.5 T 3.5 ).

e-web-492f44dfd6ec.quote: During retrieval, the system uses "Read-Priority Scheduling." Because NAND flash performance can degrade significantly if read and write operations happen simultaneously, ITME prioritizes read requests. Write operations (evictions) are deferred to periods when the model is in its "decode" phase (generating one token at a time), which typically requires less storage bandwidth than the "prefill" phase (processing the initial prompt).

e-web-4dcda68add57.quote: Figure 3: The ITME system architecture integrated with a GPU server, showing the staging buffers and the remote manager coordination.

e-web-b9eda7fdab9a.quote: The effectiveness of ITME was evaluated using Llama-3.1 models ( 8 B 8\text{B} 8 B and 70 B 70\text{B} 70 B ) across various datasets. The results highlight how tiered memory expansion can outperform traditional recomputation or standard storage-based offloading.

e-web-0dec3d88e988.quote: In scenarios where the KV cache exceeds GPU capacity, the baseline approach is often to "recompute"—discarding the cache and regenerating it from the original tokens. In testing with L l a m a - 3.1 Llama\text{-}3.1 L l ama - 3.1 8 B 8\text{B} 8 B and 70 B 70\text{B} 70 B models, ITME achieved a 1.81 × 1.81\times 1.81 × speedup in the Time To First Token (TTFT) by the fifth turn of a conversation. This demonstrates that fetching data from the CXL-hybrid memory is significantly faster than the computational cost of re-processing the input prompt.

e-web-e6efb0535453.quote: Figure 4: Normalized TTFT speedup for Llama-3.1 8B and 70B models, showing ITME's performance compared to recomputation and ideal all-caching scenarios.

e-web-5d49d64f5572.quote: One of the most striking findings occurs during extended workloads (e.g., a 35-turn conversation). In these cases, even the host memory ( T 2 T2 T 2 ) eventually runs out of space. A standard system using a 128 GB 128 \text{ GB} 128 GB host memory buffer sees its performance crash once that capacity is exhausted, reaching a 0 % 0\% 0% hit rate and falling back to recomputation speeds.

e-web-e335abe93f69.quote: In contrast, ITME maintains its performance by utilizing the TB-scale capacity of the CXL-hybrid tier. Even as the conversation grows and T 2 T2 T 2 fills up, ITME continues to serve requests from T 3.5 T3.5 T 3.5 . This resulted in a 35.7 % 35.7\% 35.7% throughput improvement over the CPU-offload baseline in the later stages of the workload.

e-web-01d06ddeec9c.quote: ITME is also effective for managing model weights that exceed GPU capacity. By prefetching model weights layer-by-layer, ITME can hide nearly all the latency associated with remote storage. For a L l a m a - 3.1 Llama\text{-}3.1 L l ama - 3.1 70 B 70\text{B} 70 B model ( 105 GB 105 \text{ GB} 105 GB of weights), the system maintained performance within 8 % 8\% 8% of a scenario where all weights were stored in expensive host DRAM, even when using only a small 4 GB 4 \text{ GB} 4 GB prefetch buffer.

e-web-6a9b7a25c3d1.quote: ITME represents a shift in how large-scale AI infrastructure can be built. Its significance lies in several key areas:

e-web-9cda2ed20a7b.quote: Economic Scaling: By using NAND flash to expand memory capacity, ITME provides a way to handle TB-scale inference states without the prohibitive cost of massive GPU clusters or high-end CPU memory configurations.

e-web-b7b87fcc7e3b.quote: Architectural Simplification: The byte-addressable nature of CXL-hybrid memory allows it to be treated as a direct extension of the system's memory pool. This removes the need for the complex file-system-based management required by traditional NVMe-oF (NVMe over Fabrics) or DPU-based solutions.

e-web-009e82d60590.quote: Predictability Exploitation: LLM workloads have highly predictable access patterns—weights are accessed layer-by-layer, and KV caches are often reused in sequence. ITME's software-hardware co-design specifically exploits this predictability to mask the inherent latencies of flash storage.

e-web-d7ed6c8cc975.quote: Hardware Feasibility: Unlike many theoretical CXL studies, ITME was validated with a physical FPGA prototype and production-grade CXL Memory Modules (CMM). This provides empirical evidence that the 18 GB/s 18 \text{ GB/s} 18 GB/s to 22 GB/s 22 \text{ GB/s} 22 GB/s bandwidth required for high-performance inference is achievable with current PCIe Gen5 technology.

e-web-ded157d6ea3c.quote: In summary, ITME offers a practical pathway for deploying massive LLMs in environments where memory capacity—rather than raw compute—is the primary constraint. By introducing a performant, byte-addressable "Shared Context Tier," it enables the long-context and agentic AI applications of the future to run efficiently on cost-effective hardware.

e-web-f63b9ecef5a1.quote: Evolution of Modern AI Inference with RAG

e-web-bc667930c1a1.quote: As AI adoption continues to grow exponentially, the AI inference market is expected to grow from USD 106.15 billion in 2025 to USD 254.9 billion by 2030 with a CAGR of 19.2% from 2025 to 2030. [1] In order to deliver accurate and timely responses, inferencing requires a different technology infrastructure stack than those used for training AI models. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a powerful technique to customize LLMs for users/use cases and can also help drive down the costs of serving up AI inference. It integrates information-retrieval with generative models to provide accurate, grounded, and context-rich responses.

e-web-737996493736.quote: RAG-based models use specific custom data to apply up-to-date knowledge that generate more accurate, relevant, and trustworthy responses. They also require storing large datasets and embeddings in memory.

e-web-0bf2cf6d6566.quote: RAG systems must maintain massive vector databases in memory for fast retrieval. These databases store high-dimensional embeddings—typically 768 to 2048 dimensions per vector—for millions or billions of data points. As organizations scale their knowledge bases and handle concurrent user queries, memory capacity and bandwidth become the primary bottlenecks.

e-web-c035bfc228cb.quote: These memory demands are compounded by the dynamic nature of RAG workloads. Memory requirements spike during data ingestion and search phases, with peak usage varying based on query volume and complexity. Simultaneous queries accessing large vector indexes require substantial memory bandwidth to maintain the low-latency responses users expect from AI applications.

e-web-f021480b9c3c.quote: Traditional server architectures face a fundamental constraint: GPU attached memory such as High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) and CPU attached memory such as DRAM are limited in capacity and cannot scale with the exponential growth of AI models and datasets due to space, thermal and cost constraints. Storage devices are used after system memory is consumed, but slower storage tiers add significant latency and impact AI performance. This “memory wall” forces difficult tradeoffs between performance, cost, and scalability. Below, Figure 2 represents an example topology. It results in:

e-web-3722bf479329.quote: Transforming LLM Inference with KV Cache

e-web-49a59528a65f.quote: The efficiency and speed of responses of AI inference models depend on how many calculations it needs to perform. They often repeat many of the same calculations, which can slow things down. Key-Value caching is a technique that helps speed up this process by remembering important information from previous steps and avoiding recomputations, resulting in much faster and more efficient responses. To avoid recomputing attention values for previously processed tokens, LLM serving systems store key-value pairs in what’s called “KV cache.” The memory requirements for this process are staggeringly high.

e-web-ae33301c639c.quote: KV cache consumes a significant amount of memory for modern LLMs—approximately 1MB of memory per token. [2] As context windows expand to 100K+ tokens—enabling analysis of multiple documents or long conversations—a single inference request can require hundreds of gigabytes of KV cache. For perspective: analyzing extended documents or maintaining long conversation histories can easily consume 1TB or more of memory just for KV cache storage. [2]

e-web-fb960571c04f.quote: Traditional memory scaling has several limitations such as:

e-web-d344795c0f12.quote: CPU storage results in low performance due to high latency

e-web-ea47f37e2a08.quote: Overhead due to limited LLM instances per server

e-web-2e14e1a831c6.quote: How Leo CXL Smart Memory Controller Solves KV Cache Memory Bottlenecks

e-web-de319981b6e6.quote: Leo CXL memory provides a high-performance tier specifically suited for KV cache storage, with several breakthrough advantages:

e-web-1243a6296928.quote: Efficient GPU Offloading : Based on real world inference workloads, CXL-CPU interconnect performs comparably to CPU-GPU interconnect for data transfer. [3] This means KV cache can be efficiently offloaded from constrained GPU memory to more abundant CXL memory without the significant latency penalties that would make this approach impractical.

e-web-8499efb72e73.quote: Increased Throughput with Consistent Performance : By storing KV cache in CXL memory rather than recomputing it, serving systems can handle 30% larger batch sizes while maintaining the same performance targets for time-to-first-token. [2] Larger batch sizes directly translate to higher throughput and better GPU utilization—critical metrics for production deployments.

e-web-5840f2d117f7.quote: Dramatic Infrastructure Cost Reduction : Production modeling demonstrates that storing KV cache on CXL memory can reduce GPU requirements by up to 87%, with 75% higher GPU utilization for the prefill stage compared to full KV recomputation. [2] This fundamentally changes the economics of LLM deployment, allowing organizations to serve more users with less infrastructure investment.

e-web-e7fa46cb76ed.quote: Enhanced Concurrent Processing : Real-world implementations show CXL enables systems to support 2× more concurrent LLM instances per server while reducing CPU utilization per query by 40%. [2] This means cloud providers and enterprises can serve more users with the same infrastructure investment, directly improving return on investment for AI deployments.

e-web-a065b8fdb3ac.quote: With Leo CXL Smart Memory Controller, AI Inference with KV cache is shown to have significant performance improvements:

This guide covers deployment planning for organizations preparing to implement CXL-based memory pooling in their AI infrastructure.

e-web-071d63752aa4.quote: CXL 4.0 enables memory pooling at unprecedented scale, allowing AI inference workloads to access 100+ terabytes of shared memory with cache coherency across multiple racks. The specification's bundled ports aggregate multiple physical connections into single logical attachments delivering 1.5 TB/s bandwidth. For infrastructure planners, the key decisions involve understanding when to adopt CXL (2026-2027 for production), which products to evaluate now (CXL 2.0/3.0 switches shipping), and how CXL complements rather than replaces NVLink and UALink. This guide provides the technical depth and decision frameworks needed to plan CXL deployments.

e-web-0c94b6e42094.quote: Large language models hit a fundamental constraint: GPU memory capacity. Modern AI inference workloads routinely exceed 80-120 GB per GPU, and the key-value (KV) cache grows with context length. 1 A single inference request with a 128K context window can consume tens of gigabytes just for KV cache storage.

e-web-326bfd7b17f6.quote: The problem intensifies at scale. Model weights for frontier LLMs consume hundreds of gigabytes. KV cache requirements grow linearly with both batch size and sequence length. GPU VRAM remains fixed at 80GB (H100) or 192GB (B200). 2

e-web-e8f691fd18b8.quote: CXL changes this equation by enabling memory pooling with DRAM-like latency (200-500 ns) across the data center. 3

e-web-9c78fee34018.quote: CXL has matured rapidly since its 2019 introduction. Each generation expanded capabilities:

e-web-cfba1c3e026a.quote: CXL 2.0 introduced the foundational concept of memory pooling. Multiple Type 3 memory devices connect to a switch, forming a shared pool from which the switch dynamically allocates resources to different hosts. 4 This enables memory utilization improvements from typical 50-60% to 85%+ across a cluster.

e-web-30367738d7e3.quote: CXL 3.0 added fabric capabilities supporting multi-level switching and up to 4,096 nodes with port-based routing (PBR). 5 The shift to 256-byte FLITs and PCIe 6.0's 64 GT/s doubled available bandwidth.

e-web-5293165b184c.quote: CXL 4.0 doubles bandwidth again while introducing features critical for multi-rack AI deployments.

e-web-4afa3b1f2b5d.quote: CXL 4.0's most significant feature for high-performance computing: bundled ports aggregate multiple physical CXL device ports into a single logical entity. 6

e-web-c31c81870ec4.quote: A host and Type 1/2 device combine multiple physical ports

e-web-fd668c418b7e.quote: System software sees a single device despite multiple physical connections

e-web-4ae794bd206f.quote: Bandwidth aggregates across all bundled ports

e-web-741b32e71c20.quote: Optimized for 256-byte FLIT mode, eliminating legacy overhead

e-web-b366658fed11.quote: For context, HBM3e memory on an H200 delivers 4.8 TB/s bandwidth. 7 A bundled CXL 4.0 connection at 1.5 TB/s represents approximately 30% of that bandwidth—sufficient for many memory expansion use cases where capacity matters more than peak bandwidth.

e-web-29cacf043088.quote: CXL 4.0 builds on PCIe 7.0's physical layer improvements: 8

e-web-4301fe63f506.quote: Feature: Add TurboQuant KV Cache Quantization for Memory-Efficient Long-Context Inference #21618

e-web-1c5e127e2d26.quote: Add support for TurboQuant KV cache quantization to enable memory-efficient long-context LLM inference with near-lossless quality.

e-web-0e27342cc938.quote: TurboQuant is a novel online vector quantization method from the Google ICLR 2026 paper "TurboQuant: Online Vector Quantization with Near-optimal Distortion Rate" ( https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.19874 ).

e-web-abfdaf055b69.quote: KV cache is typically the biggest memory consumer during LLM inference, especially for long contexts:

e-web-b2dfd2f70278.quote: A 70B model running 32k context can use 20-40GB of KV cache alone

e-web-33b1542bc2a0.quote: Current quantization options (FP8, INT4) use scalar quantization with MSE optimization

e-web-cb1456c4707a.quote: These methods don't optimize for inner product preservation , which is critical for attention mechanisms

e-web-32e38fc4014d.quote: Pre-processes KV vectors with a random orthogonal matrix to spread energy evenly across dimensions, making the Gaussian assumption valid for optimal quantization.

e-web-3e1461cc4638.quote: Uses learned codebooks (via Lloyd-Max algorithm) for near-optimal quantization of rotated vectors, beating uniform quantization on MSE.

e-web-8ca552a752ae.quote: Auto-calibrates on first batch to detect high-variance channels

e-web-4b2e725d35ed.quote: Top 15% high-variance channels (especially RoPE-affected) kept at bf16

e-web-5c7ccb9b2ca6.quote: Remaining channels quantized at 4-bit with Lloyd-Max codebooks

e-web-60b88db7d140.quote: 1-bit Johnson-Lindenstrauss correction for unbiased inner product estimation.

e-web-5df4d5e01cbe.quote: TurboQuant is a KV-cache compression method from Google Research that was presented at ICLR 2026. In the reported results, it compresses KV cache values to roughly 3–3.5 bits while reducing KV-cache memory by at least 6x and delivering up to 8x speedup in attention-logit computation on H100 GPUs.

e-web-2130db1e6608.quote: What makes TurboQuant worth paying attention to is not only the compression ratio. The bigger story is that it tries to improve the old trade-off teams have lived with for years: save memory with lower-bit KV quantization, but accept that long-context quality may degrade as compression becomes more aggressive.

e-web-4d6752a4568a.quote: In production, the KV cache is often the first scaling problem that really hurts. As prompts get longer, chats persist across many turns, or RAG systems attach more retrieved context to every request, KV-cache memory grows quickly and starts limiting concurrency, latency, and infrastructure efficiency.

e-web-400f13ef65bf.quote: That is why TurboQuant matters in practice. The challenge is no longer just “can we run the model?” but “can we run it with long context, many simultaneous sessions, and predictable cost?” TurboQuant is relevant because it targets that serving-layer bottleneck directly, without requiring retraining or fine-tuning.

e-web-24339900cc73.quote: The previous paradigm was straightforward: quantize the KV cache with lower precision, usually with traditional scalar quantization, and accept some degradation if the memory savings were worth it. That approach is still useful, but as teams push it to lower bit widths, the risk of hurting long-context behavior rises, especially in retrieval-heavy or memory-constrained workloads.

e-web-c6b9065efbd3.quote: That made deployment feel like a balancing act. Teams could lower memory usage, but they often had to wonder how much quality loss was still acceptable before the product started to feel unreliable in long chats, document QA, or agent workflows.

e-web-7b8a4ca758dd.quote: A big part of TurboQuant’s practical advantage comes from ideas Google also describes through PolarQuant. PolarQuant is a related method based on random preconditioning plus a polar transformation, and Google explicitly says TurboQuant uses PolarQuant together with QJL to achieve its results.

e-web-631076b8484c.quote: The practical point is easier to explain than the math. Traditional KV quantization often needs extra normalization metadata such as scales and zero-points stored in higher precision for each block of data. PolarQuant changes the representation first, so the resulting angles follow a concentrated and analytically predictable distribution, which reduces or removes the need for that explicit normalization overhead.

e-web-e3a46efca580.quote: That matters because the old approach did not only compress the cache; it also carried extra metadata that reduced the real savings. PolarQuant is important in this story because it helps explain why TurboQuant is not just “lower bits again,” but a more efficient compression strategy for long-context inference.

e-web-1da662d399a1.quote: The practical promise of TurboQuant is simple: more useful context capacity on the same hardware. If KV-cache memory shrinks substantially while model quality stays stable on the reported benchmarks, a serving stack can fit more active sessions per GPU, support longer contexts, or postpone an infrastructure upgrade.

e-web-b48a9e904efc.quote: This is also why TurboQuant is more than a paper result. vLLM documents TurboQuant support for KV-cache quantization, and vLLM-metal documents TurboQuant-based KV compression on Apple Silicon with 2.5x–5x KV-cache reduction and minimal quality loss, which shows the idea is already moving into real inference backends.

e-web-12e4fe6a6694.quote: The clearest early use cases are the workloads already suffering from KV-cache growth. Long-context chat, document QA, RAG systems with many retrieved chunks, agents that keep long histories, and multi-user inference APIs are the best candidates because these are the setups where memory pressure quickly becomes a product problem.

e-web-352ecfef7343.quote: That also means TurboQuant is not automatically the right answer everywhere. For short prompts, low concurrency, or batch-oriented workloads where KV memory is small, the gains may be limited and the extra compression logic may not matter much.

e-web-4a5bbd6861d9.quote: A useful way to evaluate TurboQuant is not to start from theory, but from workload behavior. The important questions are whether it improves concurrency, extends usable context length, or lowers serving cost without introducing noticeable degradation in long-context tasks.

e-web-9feaca6c44da.quote: A lightweight benchmark can still be useful, as long as it is described honestly. Metrics such as normalized reconstruction error, inner-product bias, and attention KL divergence are reasonable proxies for comparing TurboQuant with traditional scalar KV quantization, but they are still proxies. They help explain the direction of the trade-off, not replace end-to-end tests on real models and production kernels.

e-web-e17cc5244804.quote: Use TurboQuant when serving Llama 3 or Llama 3.1 Instruct with long context and many concurrent chats, where KV-cache memory starts limiting how many sessions a single GPU can sustain. In that setting, the goal is not only to save memory, but to keep long histories practical without moving too early to a larger GPU tier.

e-web-ccd6fc55fa63.quote: Use TurboQuant when running Qwen models for document QA, RAG , or retrieval-heavy assistants with 32K–128K context. These are exactly the cases where traditional low-bit KV quantization becomes harder to defend because context fidelity matters more than squeezing out a small additional memory gain.

e-web-ddfc5ec90164.quote: Use TurboQuant on Apple Silicon with vLLM-metal for smaller Llama-family deployments when the objective is to increase local context capacity while keeping quality loss limited. Use it in agent systems and long-running assistants when the accumulated history is what pushes VRAM or unified memory usage up over time.

e-web-ff2ac0938ebf.quote: Is TurboQuant mainly about speed or memory?

e-web-426b8a4fae2c.quote: It starts with memory. Google Research reports at least 6x KV-cache memory reduction and up to 8x speedup in attention-logit computation, so the speed benefit follows from making a major memory bottleneck smaller.

e-web-26e5cb675294.quote: How is it different from traditional KV quantization?

e-web-707481a800e3.quote: Traditional KV quantization usually reduces precision and accepts some degradation as part of the trade-off. TurboQuant is interesting because it aims to preserve more useful long-context quality under aggressive compression, rather than simply pushing to lower bits in the same old way.

e-web-af02cef63bff.quote: Does it require retraining the model?

e-web-df26288272c8.quote: No retraining or fine-tuning is required in the reported setup. That is part of the practical appeal, because it can be evaluated as an inference-time serving optimization rather than a model-development project.

e-web-096103f994b7.quote: Where is it already showing up?

e-web-0a6d1588851b.quote: TurboQuant is already documented in vLLM-related tooling, including the main vLLM documentation and vLLM-metal. That suggests the method is moving from research into deployable inference infrastructure.

e-web-0416df950674.quote: Which workloads should test it first?

e-web-f57f36d3e884.quote: Long-context chat, RAG, document analysis, persistent-memory agents, and multi-session inference APIs should test it first. These are the workloads most likely to feel KV-cache growth as a real bottleneck.

e-web-5474d9cf07aa.quote: Is PolarQuant the same thing as TurboQuant?

e-web-bd9981e8ed23.quote: Not exactly. PolarQuant is a related quantization method that Google also presents separately, and Google explicitly says TurboQuant uses PolarQuant together with QJL in the broader system. In practice, PolarQuant helps explain why TurboQuant can reduce normalization overhead more effectively than older scalar KV quantization methods.

e-web-4a80f86f54df.quote: The KV cache quietly becomes your VRAM bottleneck as context length grows. At 128K tokens, a 70B model's KV cache alone consumes around 40 GB, nearly double the headroom available on two H100 SXM5s after loading the model weights. TurboQuant, a new method from Google Research (arXiv 2504.19874, ICLR 2026), compresses that KV cache 6x and speeds up attention computation 8x. If you're running long-context inference or serving high-concurrency workloads, this is worth understanding now. For broader GPU memory context, see our GPU memory requirements for LLMs guide.

e-web-b5ebcc32925b.quote: TL;DR: Google TurboQuant, 6x KV Cache Compression for LLM Inference

e-web-5cc3e99331e9.quote: What it does: TurboQuant (Google Research, ICLR 2026) compresses the KV cache about 6x at 3 bits per value and reports 8x faster attention on H100; weights are unchanged.

e-web-a577fa717834.quote: Memory: a Llama 3.1 70B KV cache at 128K context drops from 40 GB to about 6.7 GB.

e-web-2c65e2508ed1.quote: Concurrency: on 2x H100 SXM5 serving 70B FP16 at 32K context, users per node rise from ~2 to ~11, cutting cost per user-hour from ~$2.64 to ~$0.48 at 12 Oct 2026 rates.

e-web-c158f6d90ee9.quote: Status: no official Google code as of Oct 2026; vLLM's FP8 KV cache ( --kv-cache-dtype fp8 , ~2x) is the production default.

e-web-d3d300b8d2ea.quote: Live rate: Spheron H100 runs $2.75/hr on-demand as of 21 Oct 2026; B200 on Spheron adds 192GB.

e-web-fcfcc8466e8c.quote: TurboQuant is a KV cache compression method, not a model weight quantization technique. This distinction matters. The model weights for a 70B model still require 140 GB of VRAM at FP16 regardless of TurboQuant. What changes is the memory footprint of the attention key-value cache generated during inference.

e-web-9f4d31be324a.quote: 6x memory reduction in KV cache versus storing in BF16, by quantizing keys and values down to as little as 3 bits per value

e-web-c5ccaeb6763a.quote: 8x speedup in attention computation measured on H100 GPUs versus 32-bit (FP32) unquantized keys (not overall inference throughput)

e-web-59a6126fd5dd.quote: Minimal accuracy loss on long-context benchmarks (LongBench, Needle In A Haystack, RULER, L-Eval). Google's own writeup calls this zero accuracy loss with perfect downstream results; independent reproductions have found more variation, covered below

e-web-633a2d25092c.quote: The critical difference from weight quantization methods like AWQ or GPTQ: TurboQuant and weight quantization address different memory pools. They are complementary, not alternatives. You can apply AWQ to compress model weights, then run TurboQuant on top to compress the KV cache at inference time.

e-web-0b675c6d373d.quote: Standard KV cache quantization (INT8 or INT4) often introduces noticeable accuracy loss because key and value vectors have irregular distributions. Outlier activations cause large quantization errors when you force these values into low-bit integers. KIVI attacks that same distribution problem differently, quantizing keys per-channel and values per-token to reach 2-bit; our KV cache quantization setup guide for KIVI's INT2 method has the install steps and the roughly one-point accuracy cost it measured.

e-web-773c171bc9ca.quote: TurboQuant uses a two-stage approach that sidesteps this problem without requiring calibration data.

e-web-75dfae254370.quote: PolarQuant applies a random rotation matrix to each key and value vector before quantization. The rotation doesn't change the mathematical content of the vectors, but it redistributes the variance uniformly across all coordinates. After rotation, the distribution of each coordinate looks much more like a standard normal, which quantizes accurately with a simple scalar quantizer. The optimal scalar quantizer for each coordinate is then computed analytically. No learned parameters, no calibration.

e-web-77ba56b2aa98.quote: After PolarQuant quantization, a 1-bit Quantized Johnson-Lindenstrauss (QJL) transform is applied as an error corrector. The QJL transform compresses the residual quantization error into a 1-bit representation using a random matrix derived from the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma. This corrector is also data-oblivious.

e-web-c2b0626e3bff.quote: Together, PolarQuant and QJL achieve the 6x KV cache compression ratio. Because the entire approach uses random (not learned) matrices, you can apply it to any model at any time without a calibration run.

e-web-7df7fc8d8095.quote: For context on why memory bandwidth is often the bottleneck in the first place, see Why Your LLM Inference Is Slow .

e-web-bea9581fe8f6.quote: These calculations use Llama 3.1 architecture parameters. "Available VRAM" assumes 2x H100 SXM5 (160 GB total) with a 70B FP16 model using 140 GB for weights, leaving 20 GB for KV cache.

e-web-371ef9b3c039.quote: The 128K row for 70B is where TurboQuant has the biggest practical impact. Without compression, a 40 GB KV cache on hardware with only 20 GB of headroom means a single 128K-context request cannot be served alongside the model weights. With TurboQuant, the 6.7 GB footprint fits comfortably, with room to serve multiple concurrent requests.

e-web-694ac0789c8c.quote: Add 10-20% headroom in production for framework buffers and activation memory beyond the KV cache figures shown above.

e-web-4beaf0cf56d9.quote: TurboQuant doesn't reduce the number of GPUs needed to load a model. But it dramatically changes how many users you can serve per GPU-hour.

e-web-e68bae022a5e.quote: Setup: 70B model at FP16 on 2x H100 SXM5 on-demand at $2.75/hr per GPU ($5.50/hr total, Spheron rates as of 21 Oct 2026). Available VRAM headroom for KV cache: 20 GB. e-web-0c34d2c4515d.quote: As of October 2026, Google Research still hasn't shipped an official Python implementation of TurboQuant. Google's own research blog post on the method restates the compression and speedup numbers but stops short of a code release, and the Google Research GitHub organization has nothing published under the TurboQuant name. The method is still described only in arXiv 2504.19874 (ICLR 2026).

e-web-c86002f2f12f.quote: What has shown up instead are unofficial, independent ports. A from-scratch PyTorch implementation with custom Triton kernels and a separate open-source port both reimplement the paper's random-rotation-plus-scalar-quantization approach, and both are explicit that they aren't affiliated with or endorsed by Google. They're useful for prototyping the idea today, but not as a production dependency. See the next section for how their own test results compare to the paper's headline numbers.

e-web-b4e8aa8c1ac7.quote: In the meantime, if you need KV cache compression today, vLLM supports FP8 KV cache quantization natively with the --kv-cache-dtype fp8 flag. It achieves roughly 2x compression versus BF16, not TurboQuant's 6x, but it's production-ready now:

e-web-cf3597b103ae.quote: For weight quantization to reduce the 140 GB model footprint itself, see our guide on FP4 quantization on Blackwell GPUs .

e-web-193fa57a8423.quote: Google's own benchmarks report zero accuracy loss at 3 bits per value and an 8x attention speedup on H100 GPUs. The two unofficial ports above are the first chance anyone outside Google has had to put those numbers to a real model, and the results land short of the headline.

e-web-09151a0eec7e.quote: The PyTorch reimplementation found that a high attention similarity score doesn't guarantee a working generation: a configuration that measured 0.9996 cosine similarity and a 94% top-1 attention match at 8K context with 5.1x compression still needed correction after an earlier "18/18 perfect generation at 5x compression" result turned out to trace back to a test bug. The separate open-source port shows the same pattern at the aggressive end of the range: its 3-bit modes showed 15-25 point drops on reasoning benchmarks at long context, while a 4-bit variant held up closer to the paper, landing around 2.6-3.1x real-world KV reduction with roughly a 1-point accuracy cost against an FP8 baseline.

e-web-e119161ec274.quote: The practical takeaway: FP8 KV cache quantization, 2x compression, already production-ready in vLLM, is still the safer default. Reach for a TurboQuant-style approach only when you specifically need more than 2x compression and can validate accuracy against your own evaluation set first, rather than trusting the paper's numbers to transfer directly to your model and context length.

e-web-4a262114080f.quote: These methods target different memory pools and are not alternatives. You can stack them.

e-web-abba5f6ff051.quote: The combination that matters for long-context inference: AWQ or GPTQ for weights, TurboQuant for KV cache. A 70B model at AWQ 4-bit needs about 35 GB for weights, fitting on a single H100 SXM5. Add TurboQuant and the 128K KV cache drops from 40 GB to 6.7 GB. Total VRAM: ~42 GB on a single 80 GB H100, with room left for batching. That's a workload that previously needed multiple GPUs running comfortably on one.

e-web-94b279953fca.quote: 01 Understand your KV cache footprint Measure how much VRAM your KV cache consumes at your target context length. At 128K context, a 70B model's KV cache alone can use around 40 GB, more than the 20 GB of headroom available on 2x H100 SXM5 after loading the model weights.

e-web-38e262a7f073.quote: 02 Apply PolarQuant rotation to key and value vectors TurboQuant's first stage applies a data-oblivious random rotation matrix (PolarQuant) to each key and value vector before quantization. This redistributes variance uniformly across coordinates without any learned parameters.

e-web-4bff9033544e.quote: 03 Apply optimal scalar quantization per coordinate After rotation, each coordinate is independently quantized using an analytically optimal scalar quantizer. This step achieves most of the 6x memory reduction.

e-web-dcac6c0ebe89.quote: 04 Apply QJL error correction A 1-bit Quantized Johnson-Lindenstrauss (QJL) transform serves as an error corrector, further reducing the approximation error in the attention computation using a random matrix derived from the JL lemma.

e-web-6625fe2e7d5d.quote: 05 Deploy with vLLM on Spheron Once an official TurboQuant implementation is available, integrate it with vLLM for GPU cloud deployment on Spheron. Provision based on model weight requirements: a 70B model still needs 2x H100 SXM5 at FP16, but TurboQuant lets that setup serve far more concurrent users at long context lengths.

e-web-af74317b1bd2.quote: TurboQuant is a KV cache compression method from Google Research that reduces KV cache memory 6x and speeds up attention computation up to 8x versus 32-bit keys. It uses PolarQuant and QJL, requires no calibration data, and is described in arXiv 2504.19874 (ICLR 2026).

e-web-d5b156911b95.quote: 02 Does TurboQuant require a calibration dataset?

e-web-23dc2d0a3f32.quote: No. TurboQuant is data-oblivious. It uses random rotation matrices (PolarQuant) followed by optimal scalar quantization, then a 1-bit QJL error corrector. No representative dataset or calibration step is needed, unlike AWQ or GPTQ.

e-web-6beb2d55dd6d.quote: 03 Which GPU should I use for models with TurboQuant?

e-web-26dedfd6a26c.quote: TurboQuant doesn't change weight VRAM requirements. A 70B model at FP16 still needs 2x H100 SXM5. TurboQuant frees up VRAM that was allocated to KV cache, letting you serve longer contexts or more concurrent users on the same hardware.

e-web-756ea2fa253c.quote: 04 How does TurboQuant compare to AWQ and GPTQ?

e-web-decbc7757570.quote: AWQ and GPTQ compress model weights. TurboQuant compresses the KV cache. They target different memory pools and can be combined: use AWQ or GPTQ for weight compression, then TurboQuant on top for KV cache compression during inference.

e-web-fc9672060753.quote: 05 Is TurboQuant available as a Python library?

e-web-224b3dee3839.quote: As of April 2026, no official Python implementation has been publicly released by Google Research. The method is described in arXiv 2504.19874 (ICLR 2026). Watch the Google Research GitHub for the official release.

agreements: TurboQuant와 ITME는 각각 소프트웨어 알고리즘 계층의 KV 캐시 압축과 하드웨어 CXL 기반 다계층 메모리 확장을 통해 LLM의 대규모 KV 캐시 및 메모리 병목 문제를 해결하려는 접근법이다.
두 기술 모두 확인된 기술성숙도가 실험실 환경 프로토타입/PoC 수준인 TRL 3 단계에 머물러 있으며, 상용 클라우드 환경 배포 및 대규모 실서빙 운영 데이터가 부재하다.
상용화 및 실제 시장 배포 현황이 미확인 상태이며, 일반 CXL 부품(SK하이닉스 CMM-DDR5 등)이나 표준화 동향 외에 개별 기술(TurboQuant, ITME)의 상용 채택 사례는 확인되지 않는다.

conflicts.why: TurboQuant의 효용성에 대해 이해관계자 간 평가가 엇갈린다. vLLM 연구팀은 FP8 대비 KV 캐시 절감 효과가 미미하고 처리량·지연시간 저하가 지속되어 도입 가치가 낮다고 평가한 반면, AMD ROCm 연구진과 Spheron은 긴 컨텍스트 에이전트 워크로드에서 캐시 적중률 향상, TTFT 단축, 동시 수용 사용자 수 확대 및 비용 절감 효과가 있다고 평가하여 실용성에 대한 견해 차이가 존재한다.

synthesis.combination_hypothesis: 본 결합 효과는 TurboQuant와 ITME를 동일 시스템에서 함께 측정한 공개 실험 근거가 없으며, 두 기술의 독립적으로 확인된 특성으로부터 도출한 추론 가설이다. TurboQuant의 저비트 양자화 압축 특성(b=2에서 내적 오차 분산 제어 및 Full-Precision 수준의 검색 점수 유지)과 ITME의 긴 컨텍스트 KV 캐시 원격 오프로드 및 CPU 스테이징·프리페치 버퍼 아키텍처를 결합할 경우, ITME 계층으로 전송·저장되는 KV 캐시의 데이터 볼륨이 줄어들어 버퍼 전송 대역폭 부담을 완화할 수 있다는 가설을 세울 수 있다. 다만, 양자화 및 역양자화에 수반되는 연산 오버헤드와 ITME 비동기 프리페치 제어 로직 간의 실질적 상호작용, 전체 지연시간 및 처리량 변화에 대한 실측 데이터는 존재하지 않는다.
